draft.title: Bias and reliability
card: A biased source shows only one side of an event. Bias often comes from who made the source and why they made it.
For example, a monk in England wrote about Viking raids on his monastery. He had lost friends and treasures, so he described the Vikings as cruel and savage.
A biased source is still useful. It shows what the writer thought and felt, but it may leave out facts that do not support their view.
To judge how reliable a source is, ask who made it, why they made it, and what they might have left out. Knowing the bias helps a historian decide how far to trust it.
draft.remember: Ask who made a source and why. Knowing the bias helps you judge how far to trust it.

a.q: Why is knowing a source's bias useful to a historian?
opts: It helps them judge how far to trust the source
It shows the source has no use as evidence
It proves that every claim in the source is false
It means the source can be treated as complete
a.why: Knowing the bias helps a historian decide how reliable a source is and what it may have left out. A biased source is not useless, because it still shows what the writer believed. It does not make every claim false.
a.clue: Bias is something to weigh, not a reason to throw the source away.

b.q: A Roman general writes an account of his own victory over a rival tribe. Which question would best help a historian judge its reliability?
opts: What did the general gain by describing the battle this way?
How many pages long is the account?
Was the account written in Latin or in another language?
Is the account older than other Roman writing?
b.why: The general wrote about his own actions, so he may have shown himself in the best light. Asking what he gained points to who made the source and why. Length, language and age do not show whether the account is one-sided.
b.clue: Think about who wrote it and why they wrote it.

a.best: It helps them judge how far to trust the source

b.best: What did the general gain by describing the battle this way?
